DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
**Verdict:** The pilot is useful, but the study misreads it, and the financial case doesn't survive correction.
- **Flats:** participation was 21%, against 66% for houses. That is not "broadly similar," and it undercuts the uniform roll-out.
- **Projection:** it uses a 64% participation rate that appears nowhere in the pilot data.
- **Treatment:** the projected tonnage exceeds Brookfield's contracted capacity, and the excess isn't costed.

Corrected, the net cost exceeds the £520,000 provisional allocation even before the missing cost lines are added.

## What holds up

- **The pilot design is sound.** It ran for six months, in mixed wards, with weekly measurement by housing type. The pilot's 20% share of flats also matches the district, which makes it a good basis for projection.
- **The table arithmetic is correct.**
  - Table 1's rates follow from its household counts (66%, 21% and 57%).
  - Table 2 sums to £733,400.
  - The vehicle figure is £990,000 over seven years, about £141,400 a year.
  - The disposal saving per tonne is £112 − £38 = £74.
- **Low contamination and falling missed-collection reports** are good signs for the operation.

## Errors

**1. Flats did not participate at a similar rate.**
Table 1 shows 66% participation for houses and 21% for flats, about a third of the rate for houses. The study's text, the author's summary and the recommendation all say the opposite. This is the hardest finding, and the study states it backwards. Flats almost certainly need a different approach: communal bins, different caddies, targeted communications. That is the norm elsewhere.

**2. The 64% participation rate has no source.**
The pilot's overall rate is 57%. Because the pilot's mix of housing matches the district's, the projection can use the pilot figures directly:

| Housing type | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ~2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ~160 |
| **Total** | **52,000** | **57%** | | **~2,870** |

So projected tonnage is about **2,870 tonnes, not 3,290**. Less food waste diverted means a smaller disposal saving.

**3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029.**
- That leaves about 1,070 tonnes a year without a contract on the corrected projection, or 1,490 on the study's own figure.
- The study doesn't say where that tonnage goes.
- The next plant is 46 miles away. That likely needs bulking at a transfer station and onward haulage, which isn't costed, and its gate fee isn't known.
- If the excess ends up incinerated, there is no saving on it at all.
- "Treatment is local" is true for only about 60% of the projected tonnage.

**4. With these corrections, the service isn't fully funded.**

| | Annual |
|---|---|
| Costs as shown in Table 2 | £733,400 |
| Saving: 1,800 t at Brookfield × £74 | −£133,200 |
| Saving on the remaining ~1,070 t | between £0 and about £79,000, less haulage |
| **Net cost** | **about £521,000 to £600,000, plus haulage** |

Even in the best case, where all 2,870 tonnes save the full £74, the net cost is about £521,000. That already slightly exceeds the £520,000 allocation, and the allocation is itself provisional.

## Costs that are missing or need checking

The author says "every cost line is shown," but a typical service budget would include several items that aren't visible here:
- **Employer on-costs.** It isn't clear whether £34,000 per operative includes National Insurance and pension. If it's salary only, add roughly 25–30%, which is about £100,000 or more.
- **Cover for leave and sickness**, supervision, and a spare vehicle.
- **The dedicated phone line and web page.**
- **Haulage or transfer** for the tonnage beyond Brookfield's capacity.
- **Up-front capital.** The £990,000 vehicle purchase falls in December 2026. Depreciation spreads the cost on paper but doesn't fund the order, so the study should say how it will be financed.

## Timing and funding risks

- **New-burdens funding.** This is "indicated" and "provisional," with a margin of £30,000 even on the study's own figures. Confirm it before committing to the vehicle order.
- **The timetable has no slack.** Vehicles delivered in March feed collections starting in the first week of April. Any delay in delivery pushes back the start date.
- **The statutory deadline.** My understanding is that councils in England were required to have weekly food waste collections in place by 31 March 2026, with transitional arrangements for some. Starting in April 2027 may already put Thornbury past that date. Check whether the Council is covered by a transitional arrangement, and say so in the study.

## Weaker claims

- **The 81% satisfaction figure** doesn't state the survey's response rate or whether non-participants were surveyed. Satisfied participants are the most likely to respond.
- **"Strong participation."** The figure is a weekly set-out rate. That's a reasonable measure, and 66% is good for houses. 21% for flats isn't.

## Suggested revisions

1. Restate the projection using the pilot's actual rates by housing type, which gives about 2,870 tonnes.
2. Design and cost a separate approach for flats, and project their tonnage under it.
3. Set out a treatment plan for tonnage beyond Brookfield's 1,800-tonne capacity until 2029, with its gate fee and haulage costs.
4. Complete the cost table: on-costs, cover, supervision, the phone line, haulage and capital financing.
5. Present the net cost against the allocation as a range, and make the vehicle order conditional on funding being confirmed.
6. Confirm the Council's position against the statutory deadline.

On the corrected figures, the Council can still decide to proceed, and may be legally required to. It shouldn't approve the roll-out on the basis that it is "fully funded," or that a single uniform service will work for flats. The evidence doesn't support either.
